## Website Directory Structure and Content Analysis

I have thoroughly explored the website directory. Here's a complete overview:

### Overall Structure

The Moltis website (`/Users/penso/.superset/worktrees/moltis/thoughtful-pint/website/`) is a **Cloudflare Worker-based static site** with multi-language support (10 languages: English, French, Chinese, Spanish, German, Italian, Portuguese, Japanese, Korean, Russian).

### Directory Layout

```
website/
├── index.html                  (Language redirector)
├── index.en.html              (Main English page, ~2400 lines)
├── index.de.html, index.fr.html, etc. (Translated versions)
├── _worker.js                  (Cloudflare Worker entry point)
├── _partials/
│   └── nav.html               (Shared navigation partial)
├── /scripts/                   (Build & utility scripts)
│   ├── build-statement.mjs
│   ├── build-i18n.mjs
│   ├── build-changelog.mjs
│   ├── dev-server.mjs
│   ├── generate-install-release-manifest.mjs
│   └── validate-i18n.mjs
├── /images/                    (SVG icons: apple.svg, linux.svg, windows.svg, docker.svg, favicon-1.svg)
├── /screenshots/               (7 main PNG screenshots + /thumbs/ subdirectory)
├── /.well-known/               (Installation manifests for discovery)
├── package.json
├── wrangler.jsonc             (Cloudflare Worker config)
├── install.sh                  (Installer script)
├── og-*.png, og-*.html        (Social media preview images)
└── Various SVG favicons and assets
```

### Key Files and Their Functions

**1. index.html** - Language Detection & Redirect
- Detects user's browser language or checks `lang` cookie
- Redirects to appropriate `index.XX.html` (11 total files)
- Uses JavaScript to detect preferred language

**2. index.en.html** - Main Website (English Version)
**Structure:**
- **Head section**: Meta tags (OG, Twitter), Tailwind CSS CDN, custom theme system
- **Body layout (Client-side SPA with 5 pages hidden/shown via JS):**

  **Page: HOME** (default)
  - Announcement banner: "Full OpenClaw import — switch in one click"
  - Hero headline: "A Rust-native claw you can trust"
  - Tagline: "One binary — sandboxed, secure, yours."
  - CTA buttons: "Get Started" and "Documentation"
  - Screenshot carousel (7 thumbnails, scrollable)
  - 3 value proposition cards:
    - Secure by design
    - Your hardware (macOS, Linux, Windows)
    - Full-featured (Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, Teams, voice, memory, tools)

  **Page: INSTALL**
  - Installation tabs: curl, Homebrew, Docker, Source, Others
  - Docker command with volume mappings
  - Platform cards: macOS (Apple Silicon & Intel), Linux (x86_64 & ARM64), Windows (x86_64)
  - Cloud deployment section with DigitalOcean button
  - Fly.io deployment with random app name generation and copy-to-clipboard

  **Page: FEATURES**
  - 12 feature cards in 2/3 column grid:
    - Single Binary, Local LLMs, Authentication, Sandboxed Browsing
    - SSRF Protected, Streaming-first, Skills/Hooks/MCP
    - Memory, Voice, Sandboxed Execution, Tool Result Validation, OAuth 2.0
  - Each card has icon + title + description

  **Page: SECURITY**
  - Feature/security comparison table (5 columns: Feature, OpenClaw, NanoClaw, ZeroClaw, Moltis)
  - Rows: WebAuthn, OAuth 2.0, API keys, SSRF, WebSocket origin, Hook gating, Rate limiting
  - Performance comparison table
  - Metrics: Dist size, Cold start, RAM, Min hardware

  **Page: COMPARE**
  - Comparison charts/tables vs other solutions

  **Footer (always visible)**
  - Alpha software warning (amber banner)
  - Links: GitHub, Discord, built by Fabien Penso
  - MIT License

**3. _worker.js** - Cloudflare Worker Edge Logic
- Language detection from Accept-Language header
- Cookie-based lang preference fallback
- Partial injection: replaces `<!--NAV-->` comment with nav.html content
- Routes "/" to appropriate `index.XX.html` based on language
- Falls back to static asset serving

**4. _partials/nav.html** - Shared Navigation Component
```html
<nav class="sticky top-0"> structure with:
- Logo + "Moltis" gradient text
- Desktop nav tabs: Home, Install, Features, Security, Compare, Changelog
- Mobile scrollable tabs
- Theme toggle (light/system/dark cycle)
- Language selector dropdown (10 options with HTML entities)
- GitHub stars badge (fetches count from GitHub API)
```

**5. package.json** - Build Configuration
```json
Scripts:
- "build": runs build-statement.mjs + build-changelog.mjs
- "build:changelog": generates changelog
- "install-manifest:update": generates release manifests
- "i18n:validate": validates i18n consistency
Dependencies: jsdom 28.1.0
```

**6. wrangler.jsonc** - Cloudflare Worker Config
- Name: "withered-breeze-e956"
- Entry point: _worker.js
- Assets binding: root directory as ASSETS
- Observability: logging enabled, tracing disabled

**7. scripts/build-statement.mjs** - Markdown to HTML Builder
- Converts `statement.md` → `statement/index.html`
- Custom markdown parser (headings, lists, code, inline formatting)
- Generates styled HTML with orange/red theme

### Design & Technology Stack

**Frontend:**
- **CSS Framework**: Tailwind CSS (CDN version)
- **Theme System**: Light/Dark/System with localStorage persistence
- **Fonts**: Space Grotesk (sans), JetBrains Mono (mono), Outfit (headings)
- **Animations**: Custom pulse-slow animation (0.3-0.7 opacity), 4s cycle
- **Responsive Design**: Mobile-first with sm/md/lg breakpoints

**Interactivity (Vanilla JS):**
- Page routing via hash navigation (#home, #install, etc.)
- Install tab switching (curl/brew/docker/source/others)
- Theme toggle cycle (3 modes)
- Language switcher (cookie-based, page reload)
- Lightbox gallery (7 screenshots with arrow nav + keyboard controls)
- Fly.io command generation with clipboard copy + toast notification
- Screenshot carousel (horizontal scroll with gradient fade edges)

**Build System:**
- Node.js scripts (ESM modules)
- jsdom for DOM parsing/testing
- npm run scripts for build, validation

**Deployment:**
- Cloudflare Workers (serverless edge function)
- Static assets served from same directory
- Worker runs before assets, injects nav partial
- HTTPS default, handles language negotiation at edge

### Current Features Highlighted

1. **Multi-language**: 10 languages + fallback to browser preference
2. **Screenshot Gallery**: 7 images with lightbox, carousel thumbnail view
3. **Installation Methods**: 5 different install options (curl, brew, Docker, source, others)
4. **Platform Support**: macOS, Linux, Windows with architecture details
5. **Cloud Deploy**: DigitalOcean one-click, Fly.io with custom naming
6. **Comparison Tables**: Security features, performance metrics vs competitors
7. **Theme Support**: Full light/dark mode toggle with system preference detection
8. **Responsive Design**: Mobile/tablet/desktop optimization

### Static Assets

**Images:**
- Favicons: favicon.svg, favicon-512.png, favicon-512.svg, favicon-compact-512.png
- Platform icons: apple.svg, linux.svg, windows.svg, docker.svg
- Social preview: og-image.jpg/png, og-social.jpg/png, github-avatar.png/svg, twitter-announce.png
- Screenshots: 7 full-res PNGs (1-7.png) + 7 thumbnails in /thumbs/

**Metadata Files:**
- .well-known/moltis-install.json (stable manifest)
- .well-known/moltis-install/channels/stable.json (moving pointer)
- Install release manifest generation script

**Other:**
- CHANGELOG.md
- llms.txt (likely LLM discovery info)
- releases.json (release manifest)

This is a well-structured, modern website using Tailwind CSS, Cloudflare Workers for edge serving, multi-language support, and progressive enhancement with vanilla JavaScript. All pages are built from a single HTML template with client-side routing.

Here is a thorough analysis of the Polyphony.to website's pill/badge design patterns.

---

## Overall Page Structure (10 sections, top to bottom)

| # | Section | id | Key Pattern |
|---|---------|-----|-------------|
| 0 | Hero | (none) | "Git-Native AI Orchestration" + Alpha badge |
| 1 | Problem | (none) | Two-column comparison |
| 2 | How It Works | `how-it-works` | 4-step numbered walkthrough |
| 3 | Get Started | `install` | Platform-tabbed install commands |
| 4 | Why Polyphony | `features` | Three-pillar value props |

| 7 | See It in Action | (none) | Three showcase cards |
| 8 | **Works with Your Stack** | `agents` | **The pill/badge section** |

## 1. Integration Pills ("Works with Your Stack" section)

### HTML Structure

Two rows, each with a category label and a `flex-wrap` row of pill elements:

```html
<section id="agents" class="py-32">
  <div class="max-w-6xl mx-auto px-6 text-center">
    <h2>Works with your stack</h2>
    <p>Connect any tracker and dispatch to any agent.</p>

    <div class="space-y-12">
      <!-- Row 1 -->
      <div data-animate>
        <p class="text-xs uppercase tracking-widest text-muted mb-6">Issue Trackers</p>
        <div class="flex flex-wrap items-center justify-center gap-6">
          <div class="integration-icon glass-card px-6 py-4 flex items-center gap-3 text-sm font-medium">
            <img src="assets/icons/github.svg" alt="GitHub" class="w-6 h-6 icon-auto-invert"> GitHub
          </div>
          <!-- ...GitLab, Linear, Beads -->
        </div>
      </div>

      <!-- Row 2 -->
      <div data-animate>
        <p class="text-xs uppercase tracking-widest text-muted mb-6">AI Agents</p>
        <div class="flex flex-wrap items-center justify-center gap-6">
          <div class="integration-icon glass-card px-6 py-4 flex items-center gap-3 text-sm font-medium">
            <img src="assets/icons/claude.svg" alt="Claude" class="w-6 h-6"> Claude
          </div>
          <!-- ...Codex, Copilot, Pi, OpenAI-compatible, ACP -->
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>
```

**Items displayed:**
- **Issue Trackers row:** GitHub, GitLab, Linear, Beads
- **AI Agents row:** Claude, Codex, Copilot, Pi, OpenAI-compatible, ACP

Each pill is: `[icon 24x24] [label text]` inside a `div`.

### Category Labels

Uppercase micro-labels above each row:
```
text-xs uppercase tracking-widest text-muted mb-6
```
Renders as small, spaced-out, muted gray text like "ISSUE TRACKERS" and "AI AGENTS".

---

## 2. CSS for the Pills

### `.glass-card` (the frosted-glass pill base)

```css
.glass-card {
  background: var(--glass-bg);
  backdrop-filter: blur(12px);
  border: 1px solid var(--glass-border);
  border-radius: 12px;
  transition: border-color 0.3s, box-shadow 0.3s, background-color 0.3s;
}

.glass-card:hover {
  border-color: rgba(124, 58, 237, 0.3);          /* purple tint */
  box-shadow: 0 0 30px rgba(124, 58, 237, 0.05);  /* purple glow */
}
```

### `.integration-icon` (the pill behavior layer)

```css
.integration-icon {
  transition: transform 0.2s, opacity 0.2s;
  opacity: 0.6;                /* muted by default */
}

.integration-icon:hover {
  transform: scale(1.1);       /* pop up slightly */
  opacity: 1;                  /* full brightness */
}
```

### Computed values at rest (light mode)

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| padding | `16px 24px` |
| border-radius | `12px` |
| border | `1px solid rgba(0,0,0,0.08)` |
| background | `rgba(0,0,0,0.03)` |
| backdrop-filter | `blur(12px)` |
| font-size | `14px` |
| font-weight | `500` (medium) |
| color | `#1a1a2e` |
| opacity | `0.6` (muted at rest) |
| display | `flex` |
| gap | `12px` |

### CSS Custom Properties (theme-aware)

**Light mode (`:root`):**
```css
--glass-bg: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.03);
--glass-border: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.08);
--icon-invert: 0;
--text-primary: #1a1a2e;
```

**Dark mode (`.dark`):**
```css
--glass-bg: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.03);
--glass-border: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
--icon-invert: 1;
--text-primary: #e5e5ef;
```

### Icon dark-mode handling

Two strategies:
1. **`icon-auto-invert`** class: uses `filter: invert(var(--icon-invert))` so icons auto-flip between light/dark
2. **Inline `style="filter: ..."`** on individual icons: per-icon hue-rotation to colorize monochrome SVGs (e.g., GitLab gets orange, Linear gets purple)

---

## 3. Scroll-Reveal Animations

The pill groups are wrapped in `data-animate` containers. An `IntersectionObserver` adds `animate-in` when they enter view:

```css
[data-animate] {
  opacity: 0;
  transform: translateY(24px);
  transition: opacity 0.6s ease-out, transform 0.6s ease-out;
}

[data-animate].animate-in {
  opacity: 1;
  transform: translateY(0);
}
```

Staggered children (if wrapped in `data-animate-stagger`) get 100ms incremental delays (nth-child 1 through 6).

---

## 4. Hero "Alpha" Badge

A second badge pattern appears in the hero, using a fully-rounded pill shape:

```html
<div class="inline-flex items-center gap-2 px-4 py-1.5 rounded-full
            border border-amber-400/30 bg-amber-500/10 text-xs font-medium">
  Alpha
  Experimental -- actively developed, expect breaking changes
</div>
```

This is a different style from the integration pills: **fully-rounded** (`rounded-full` = `border-radius: 9999px`), amber-colored border and background, smaller text (`text-xs`).

---

## 5. Design Pattern Summary

The key design decisions:

1. **Glassmorphism pills** -- subtle translucent background (`rgba(0,0,0,0.03)`), `backdrop-filter: blur(12px)`, and `12px` border-radius. Not fully rounded pills, more like rounded rectangles.

2. **Muted-by-default, vivid-on-hover** -- pills sit at `opacity: 0.6` and scale + brighten to full on hover. This keeps the section visually calm while still being interactive.

3. **Purple accent on hover** -- the accent color `#7c3aed` (Tailwind violet-600) appears as a subtle border color and glow on hover, unifying the hover state across the entire site.

4. **Icon + text, no background color per pill** -- all pills share the same glass background. Brand identity comes from the SVG icon, not from coloring the pill itself.

5. **Centered flex-wrap layout** with `gap-6` (24px) between pills. Two grouped rows separated by `space-y-12` with uppercase micro-labels.

6. **Theme-adaptive** via CSS custom properties -- the same glass-card style works in both light and dark mode by swapping the variable values.

7. **Scroll-reveal** via `data-animate` + IntersectionObserver adds a polished fade-up-from-below entrance.

    79→	if (ext === ".html") {
    80→		let html = body.toString("utf8");
    81→		if (html.includes("<!--NAV-->")) {
    82→			const nav = await loadNav();
    83→			html = html.replace("<!--NAV-->", nav);
    84→		}
    85→		body = html;
    86→	}
    87→
    88→	res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": contentType });
    89→	res.end(body);
    90→});
    91→
    92→// Invalidate nav cache on file change (for live editing)
    93→import { watch } from "node:fs";
    94→watch(path.join(root, "_partials"), { recursive: true }, () => {
    95→	navCache = null;
    96→});
    97→
    98→server.listen(port, () => {
    99→	process.stdout.write(`Website dev server: http://localhost:${port}\n`);
   100→});
   101→

Here is a detailed analysis of the Hermes Agent landing page at `https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com`:

---

## 1. Headline / Tagline

**Primary tagline:** "An agent that grows with you."

This is a deliberately organic, relational framing -- not about raw capability or speed, but about a long-term relationship between the user and the agent.

---

## 2. How They Explain the Product

They lead with a **negation strategy** -- defining the product by what it is NOT before saying what it is:

> "It's not a coding copilot tethered to an IDE or a chatbot wrapper around a single API."

Then the positive definition:

> "An autonomous agent that lives on your server, remembers what it learns, and gets more capable the longer it runs."

Key phrases that carry the messaging:
- "Persistent memory and auto-generated skills -- it learns your projects and never forgets"
- "Natural language cron scheduling for reports, backups, and briefings"
- "Isolated subagents with their own conversations, terminals, and Python RPC scripts"

This positions the product as **stateful, self-improving, and server-native** -- three attributes that directly contrast with the ephemeral, cloud-dependent, IDE-bound competitors.

---

## 3. Page Sections (in order)

1. **Navigation bar** -- Install, Features, Docs, GitHub, Discord
2. **Hero section** -- ASCII art "HERMES AGENT" logo + "Open Source / MIT License" badge + core tagline
3. **Problem/Positioning statement** -- The negation-then-definition paragraph
4. **Installation CTA** -- One-line bash install script + "Sign Up on Nous Portal" button
5. **Getting Started (5-step guide)** -- Install, Configure, Chat, Enable multi-platform gateway, Update
6. **"See it in action" video** -- Embedded demo video
7. **Features section (7 subsections):**
   - Lives Where You Do (multi-platform)
   - Grows the Longer It Runs (persistent learning)
   - Scheduled Automations (cron)
   - Delegates & Parallelizes (subagents)
   - Real Sandboxing (isolation)
   - Full Web & Browser Control
   - "More details" expandable link
8. **Technical specification breakdown** -- Tools (40+), Platforms (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp/Signal/Email/CLI), Environments (Local/Docker/SSH/Modal/Daytona/Singularity), Skills (40+ bundled, agentskills.io format), Research capabilities (Atropos RL, ShareGPT export)
9. **Footer** -- "Built by Nous Research / MIT License / 2026"

---

## 4. Unique Design Patterns

- **ASCII art branding** -- Signals "developer-first" and "terminal-native" identity. This is a deliberate aesthetic choice that filters for their target audience.
- **Command-line examples as UI** -- The getting-started section shows actual CLI commands (`hermes setup`, `hermes model`), doubling as both documentation and trust signal.
- **Negation-first positioning** -- Opening by naming what you are NOT is uncommon on landing pages. It anchors the reader's mental model before the pitch.
- **Capability quantification** -- "40+" repeated for both tools and skills. Specific enough to impress, round enough to not need constant updating.
- **Friction-removal language** -- "No prerequisites," "No sudo needed," transparency about experimental Windows builds.
- **5-step from zero to multi-platform** -- Compresses perceived complexity into a manageable number.

---

## 5. Competitive Differentiation

They draw two explicit contrasts:

| Competitor archetype | Hermes counter-position |
|---|---|
| "Coding copilot tethered to an IDE" (Cursor, Copilot, etc.) | Server-based, runs anywhere, not IDE-locked |
| "Chatbot wrapper around a single API" (ChatGPT wrappers, etc.) | Multi-provider, persistent memory, autonomous |

Implicit differentiation axes:
- **Stateful vs stateless** -- Memory and learned skills persist across sessions
- **Self-hosted vs cloud-dependent** -- Lives on your server
- **Multi-channel vs single-channel** -- One agent gateway for Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, Email, CLI
- **Autonomous vs reactive** -- Cron scheduling, subagent delegation, background tasks
- **Research-backed vs product-only** -- Atropos RL integration, ShareGPT export, trajectory generation for fine-tuning
- **Open source (MIT)** -- Maximum permissiveness, vs proprietary or restrictive licenses

---

## 6. Narrative Arc

The page follows a clear persuasion structure:

1. **Emotional hook** -- "An agent that grows with you" (relational, aspirational)
2. **Problem validation via negation** -- Names the pain of IDE lock-in and API wrappers
3. **Solution definition** -- Autonomous, server-native, learning agent
4. **Friction removal** -- One-line install, 5 steps to running
5. **Proof** -- Video demo ("See it in action")
6. **Feature depth** -- 7 capability sections with concrete details
7. **Technical legitimacy** -- Environments, integrations, research capabilities
8. **Ecosystem confidence** -- MIT license, Nous Research backing, community integrations (ClawHub, LobeHub, agentskills.io)

The overall arc moves from **emotional differentiation** to **problem acknowledgment** to **rapid implementation** to **capability validation** to **ecosystem trust**. It is structured to convert both the "show me the vision" reader (top half) and the "show me the specs" reader (bottom half).

Here is a detailed analysis of the Conductor landing page at conductor.build:

---

## 1. Headline and Tagline

- **Primary headline:** "Run a team of coding agents on your Mac."
- **Subheadline:** "Create parallel Codex + Claude Code agents in isolated workspaces. See at a glance what they're working on, then review and merge their changes."

The headline is concise and action-oriented. It frames the product around a metaphor -- you are the manager of a "team" of AI agents -- which positions the developer as a conductor/orchestrator rather than a hands-on coder.

## 2. Product Explanation

Conductor is a **macOS desktop application** that lets developers run multiple AI coding agents (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex) in parallel, each in its own isolated git worktree workspace. The developer monitors all agents from a unified interface, then reviews and merges their changes. It targets full-stack engineers and teams who want to parallelize coding work across multiple tasks or repos simultaneously.

Key technical details surfaced:
- Uses **git worktrees** for workspace isolation (not containers or VMs)
- Runs **entirely locally** on the user's Mac
- Works with existing **Claude Pro/Max subscriptions** or API keys (no new billing relationship required)

## 3. Page Sections in Order

| # | Section | Content |
|---|---------|---------|
| 1 | **Hero** | Headline + subheadline, two CTAs ("Download Conductor" primary, "Learn how it works" secondary), large app screenshot |
| 2 | **Trust Bar** | "Trusted by builders at" with logos: Linear, Vercel, Notion, Stripe, Life360, Blacksmith, Reducto, Tigris |
| 3 | **Testimonials** | ~10 individual quotes from engineers/founders with name, title, company. Appears to use a carousel or multi-view layout. |
| 4 | **How It Works** | Numbered 3-step process: (1) Add your repo, (2) Deploy agents, (3) Conduct -- monitor, review, merge |
| 5 | **FAQ** | Three questions covering git worktrees, supported agents, and subscription/billing model |
| 6 | **Final CTA** | "We built Conductor using Conductor" dogfooding statement + Download button |
| 7 | **Footer** | Four columns: Company (Blog, Changelog, Join Us), Resources (Docs, Changelog), Legal (Privacy, Terms), Connect (X, YouTube, Reddit). Copyright to Melty Labs, 2026. |

The page also includes a **Series A funding announcement** callout and a **version number** (0.46.0) signaling active development.

## 4. Unique Design Patterns

- **3-step numbered explainer:** Reduces perceived complexity. Each step is one short sentence. This is the entire "education" section -- they keep it extremely minimal.
- **Testimonial saturation early:** Social proof comes *before* the product explanation, which is unusual. They lead with credibility rather than features.
- **"We built X using X" closing:** The dogfooding message ("We built Conductor using Conductor") serves as both a confidence signal and a memorable closer. It is the final thing before the download CTA.
- **No pricing section:** They avoid pricing entirely -- the product works with existing Claude/Codex subscriptions, so they sidestep the billing conversation completely.
- **No feature grid or comparison table:** Unlike most developer tool landing pages, there is no feature matrix. The entire pitch fits in about 5 short sections.
- **Version number visible:** Showing v0.46.0 signals rapid iteration and active development.

## 5. Social Proof

**Company logos (8):** Linear, Vercel, Notion, Stripe, Life360, Blacksmith, Reducto, Tigris -- a strong mix of developer-beloved companies.

**Testimonials (~10)** with notable themes:
- Productivity framing: "new productivity unlock"
- Tool displacement: "So much better than VSCode", "Is Conductor the new Cursor?"
- Emotional intensity: "last time I felt this strongly about a developer tool was Vercel and Supabase" (from a Stripe engineer)
- Indispensability: "can't imagine building without it"

The testimonials are strategically chosen to position Conductor as a replacement for existing editors/IDEs (VSCode, Cursor), not just an add-on.

## 6. Competitive Differentiation

Conductor differentiates on several axes, mostly implicit rather than through direct competitor callouts:

| Differentiator | Implicit Competitor |
|---|---|
| **Multiple agents in parallel** | Cursor, Windsurf (single-agent at a time) |
| **Runs locally on your Mac** | Cloud-based agent platforms |
| **Uses your existing subscriptions** | Tools that require new billing |
| **Git worktree isolation handled for you** | Manual worktree management |
| **Orchestration layer, not an editor** | VSCode, Cursor (editors with AI bolted on) |

The testimonial "Is Conductor the new Cursor?" is placed deliberately -- they let a user say the comparison rather than making it themselves, which is more credible.

## 7. Overall Narrative Arc

The page follows a **credibility-first** structure:

1. **Hook** -- Clear, simple value prop (one sentence)
2. **Prove it** -- Logos and testimonials immediately (before explaining how it works)
3. **Explain** -- Minimalist 3-step process
4. **Handle objections** -- FAQ on technical concerns
5. **Close** -- Dogfooding proof + download CTA

This is a notably short and confident page. There are no feature grids, no pricing tables, no lengthy comparisons. The strategy appears to be: say one thing clearly, prove others love it, make it easy to try. The entire page could be read in under 2 minutes.

**Parent company:** Melty Labs (the same team behind the Melty open-source AI code editor).

Here is the detailed analysis of the openclaw.ai landing page:

---

## OpenClaw Landing Page Analysis

### 1. Headline & Tagline

- **Main headline:** "OpenClaw -- Personal AI Assistant"
- **Tagline:** "The AI that actually does things."
- **Sub-description:** "Clears your inbox, sends emails, manages your calendar, checks you in for flights. All from WhatsApp, Telegram, or any chat app you already use."

The tagline is punchy and positions against the common complaint that AI chatbots are passive -- they answer questions but don't take action. The sub-description immediately grounds this with concrete, relatable use cases.

### 2. Product Explanation

They describe the product through action-oriented language:
- "The AI that actually does things" (core promise)
- "Runs on Your Machine" (ownership/privacy angle)
- "Any Chat App" (accessibility -- use what you already have)
- "Full System Access" (power)
- "Persistent Memory" (it becomes "uniquely yours")
- "Personal OS" framing (broader than just a chatbot)

The explanation strategy is **capability-first**: they show what it can do rather than explaining how it works technically.

### 3. Page Sections (in order)

1. **Hero** -- Headline, tagline, description
2. **Featured Partnership** -- "OpenClaw Partners with VirusTotal for Skill Security" (trust/security signal)
3. **What People Say** -- 75+ user testimonials from Twitter/X with profile pictures
4. **Quick Start / Installation** -- One-liner install commands (`curl`, `npm`), macOS companion app (beta), platform support note
5. **What It Does** -- Six capability cards (Runs on Your Machine, Any Chat App, Persistent Memory, Browser Control, Full System Access, Skills & Plugins)
6. **Works With Everything** -- 50+ integration logos (WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Slack, Signal, iMessage, Claude, GPT, Spotify, Hue, Gmail, GitHub, etc.)
7. **Featured In** -- Media mentions (MacStories by Federico Viticci, StarryHope)
8. **Community CTAs** -- Discord, Documentation, GitHub, ClawHub links
9. **Newsletter signup** -- "Stay in the Loop"
10. **Sponsors** -- Logos: OpenAI, GitHub, NVIDIA, Vercel, Blacksmith, Convex
11. **Footer** -- Blog, Showcase, Shoutouts, Integrations, Trust links. Attribution to Peter Steinberger & community. Disclaimer: "Formerly known as Clawdbot and Moltbot. Independent project, not affiliated with Anthropic."

### 4. Unique Design Patterns

- **Testimonials before features.** This is unusual -- social proof appears *above* the product explanation. They lead with community enthusiasm rather than a feature pitch. 75+ tweets is a lot of social proof for an open-source project.
- **No demo video or interactive widget on the landing page.** The product sells through user stories rather than a polished demo.
- **Install-first flow.** The Quick Start section presents installation commands prominently, treating it like a developer tool rather than a SaaS product.
- **Integration grid.** 50+ integration logos presented visually, emphasizing breadth.
- **Lobster/crustacean branding.** Self-aware humor throughout ("lobster wisdom" in the newsletter copy, the mascot "Molty").

### 5. Social Proof & Differentiation

**Social proof elements:**
- 75+ Twitter/X testimonials with real usernames and profile pictures
- Two press features (MacStories, StarryHope)
- Sponsor logos (OpenAI, GitHub, NVIDIA, Vercel, Blacksmith, Convex)
- VirusTotal partnership announcement
- No visible GitHub star count or download numbers on the page

**How they differentiate (mostly through user testimonials):**
- **vs. corporate AI (Anthropic, OpenAI SaaS):** "A megacorp like Anthropic or OpenAI could not build this. Literally impossible with how corpo works." Emphasis on local control, open source, data stays on your machine.
- **vs. Siri/traditional assistants:** "Everything Siri was supposed to be. And it goes so much further."
- **vs. SaaS tools:** "Your context and skills live on YOUR computer, not a walled garden."
- **Core differentiators:** open-source, self-hostable, runs locally, works through existing chat apps, extensible with community skills, supports multiple LLM providers (not locked to one).

### 6. CTAs

Primary CTAs are installation commands and "Download for macOS." Secondary CTAs link to Discord (community), Documentation, GitHub (source), and ClawHub (skills). There is no "Sign Up" or "Get Started" button typical of SaaS -- it's a developer/open-source install flow.

### 7. Pricing

None mentioned. It is an open-source project with no visible monetization on the landing page.

### 8. Overall Messaging Strategy

The messaging follows a **community-validated, action-oriented** strategy:
1. Make a bold promise ("actually does things")
2. Prove it immediately with user testimonials (before even explaining features)
3. Show how easy it is to install
4. List capabilities broadly
5. Demonstrate ecosystem breadth (integrations)
6. Provide external validation (press, sponsors)
7. Invite to community

The tone is enthusiastic, technically confident but casual, with self-aware humor (the lobster theme). It reads as a passion project that grew a community, not a corporate product launch.

Here is the detailed analysis of the Polyphony.to landing page:

---

## Page Structure and Content Analysis

### 1. Headline / Tagline

- **Main headline:** "Git-Native AI Orchestration"
- **Subheadline:** "Turn repository events into orchestrated agent work, from issues, PRs, webhooks, or schedules."
- **Supporting line:** "Works with GitHub, GitLab, Linear -- Supports Claude, Codex, Copilot, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Kimi, Pi, and more"
- **Status badge:** "Alpha Experimental -- actively developed, expect breaking changes"

The positioning is clear and specific: this is not a general AI tool, it is a git-native orchestration layer for coding agents. The tagline immediately communicates _where_ it lives (your repo) and _what_ it does (turns events into agent work).

---

### 2. Problem Section ("The problem with AI agents today")

This is a **two-column before/after comparison** -- "Without Polyphony" vs "With Polyphony" -- using negative (pain) and positive (solution) bullet lists.

**Without Polyphony (6 pain points):**
1. Manually copy-paste issues into agent prompts
2. Agents work in same branch, causing merge conflicts
3. No visibility until agents finish (or fail silently)
4. Failed runs require manual intervention
5. No budget controls -- runaway token usage
6. Locked into a single agent provider

**With Polyphony (6 mirrored solutions):**
1. Issues automatically pulled and dispatched
2. Isolated git worktrees -- zero conflicts
3. Live TUI dashboard with real-time progress
4. Automatic retry with configurable fallback chains
5. Token budgets, concurrency limits, cost-aware throttling
6. Multi-agent support across providers

This is a classic "problem-solution mirror" pattern. Each pain point maps 1:1 to a solution. The framing headline ("Managing AI coding agents manually does not scale") sets up the core thesis.

---

### 3. Section Order (top to bottom)

1. **Nav** -- How It Works, Features, Dashboard, Agents, GitHub
2. **Hero** -- Headline, subheadline, two CTAs (Get Started / View on GitHub), hero image placeholder
3. **Problem** -- Before/after comparison grid
4. **How It Works** -- 4 numbered steps with code/terminal snippets
5. **Installation** -- Tabbed (macOS / Linux / Windows / Source) with install commands
6. **Why Polyphony** -- 3 pillars (Issue->Agent->PR, Multi-Agent, Repo-Native)
7. **Built for Real Workflows** -- 9-feature grid (Isolated Workspaces, Retry & Fallback, Budget Control, Workflow Policy, Live Observability, Handoff Automation, Multi-Tracker, Agent Profiles, Concurrent Execution)
8. **Dashboard** -- Full TUI mockup with 3 tabs (Inbox, Runs, Agents) showing sample data tables
9. **See It in Action** -- 3 screenshot placeholders with captions
10. **Works With Your Stack** -- Logo grid (Trackers: GitHub/GitLab/Linear/Beads; Agents: Claude/Codex/Copilot/Pi/OpenAI-compatible/ACP)
11. **Built in the Open** -- Open source pitch (MIT, Rust, no telemetry), CTAs to Star/Browse Issues
12. **Footer** -- Product links, Developer links, Community links, attribution

---

### 4. Unique Design Patterns

**a) Terminal/TUI Mockups (ASCII art in the page)**
The page uses inline terminal mockups extensively -- not screenshots, but styled text that looks like terminal output. This appears in:
- The "How It Works" steps (YAML config, polling output, ASCII dashboard table, push/PR output)
- The full Dashboard section with 3 complete tabbed tables (Inbox, Runs, Agents) showing realistic data with spinners, checkmarks, and status indicators

This is a distinctive choice -- it communicates "this is a terminal-first tool" through the medium itself.

**b) Four-step "How It Works" with alternating code and prose**
Each step (Configure, Orchestrate, Monitor, Ship) pairs a description paragraph with a code/terminal snippet. Steps are numbered (01-04). The snippets are concrete: real YAML config, real terminal output with unicode spinners, a real ASCII dashboard mockup, and real git push/PR output.

**c) Tabbed Installation**
Platform-specific install commands (brew, curl, irm, cargo) in a tabbed interface. Each tab has one command and a one-line description.

**d) Problem Section as a before/after grid**
Rather than a paragraph explaining the problem, they use a visual negative/positive list comparison. This is punchy and scannable.

**e) "Three Pillars" philosophy section**
The "Why Polyphony" section distills the value proposition into three conceptual pillars rather than features: Issue->Agent->PR (lifecycle), Multi-Agent (flexibility), Repo-Native (philosophy, referencing OpenAI Symphony's WORKFLOW.md pattern).

---

### 5. How They Show the Workflow

The "How It Works" section uses a **4-step numbered progression**:

1. **Configure** -- Show YAML config (tracker + agents + workspace mode). Message: "Configuration lives in your repo as YAML -- version-controlled and reviewable."
2. **Orchestrate** -- Show terminal polling output. Message: "Polyphony polls for issues, creates isolated git worktrees, and dispatches the right agent to each task."
3. **Monitor** -- Show ASCII TUI dashboard mockup. Message: "The live TUI dashboard shows agent progress, retries, and results in real time."
4. **Ship** -- Show terminal output of commit/push/PR. Message: "Agents commit, push, and open pull requests automatically. The feedback loop is closed."

The progression tells a complete story: config -> automated dispatch -> live monitoring -> automated delivery. Each step has a code artifact that makes it concrete rather than abstract.

---

### Design and Technical Notes

- **Color scheme:** Dark mode with purple accent (#7c3aed), amber for highlights (#f59e0b)
- **Fonts:** Inter (body), JetBrains Mono (code/terminal)
- **Framework:** Tailwind CSS
- **Open source positioning:** MIT license, "no vendor lock-in, no telemetry, no hidden costs" -- the open source pitch is at the bottom, not the top, which keeps the hero focused on the product value rather than the license
- **Attribution:** "Made with love by Fabien Penso" with link to pen.so

The page is currently in an early/alpha state -- several sections reference placeholder images (1200x700 hero, 600x400 step images, 800x500 action screenshots) that haven't been replaced with real assets yet.

### Potential Challenges

- **Page length on mobile**: Adding 4 sections will make the home page significantly longer on small screens. The use cases grid (2-col on mobile) and how-it-works (1-col stack on mobile) should still feel navigable, but it is worth verifying scroll depth.

- **i18n string collision**: The `build-i18n.mjs` system does simple string replacement. Unique phrases reduce collision risk, but some short strings like "Install" already appear multiple times on the page. The new step 1 heading "Install" is already used as a nav tab, so the translation pair must be scoped carefully (e.g., using the surrounding HTML context: `">Install</h3>"`).

- **No new CSS needed**: All new sections reuse existing Tailwind classes and existing `style.css` patterns. No new custom CSS classes are required.

- **No new JS needed**: None of the new sections require interactive behavior. The `data-reveal` scroll animation could optionally be added to Section B and Section C for visual polish, since it already exists on the pills section.

  1055→  const highlightClass = "w-full text-left px-3 py-1.5 text-xs font-semibold text-orange-600 dark:text-orange-400 hover:bg-gray-100 dark:hover:bg-gray-700";
  1056→  const normalClass = "w-full text-left px-3 py-1.5 text-xs text-gray-600 dark:text-gray-300 hover:bg-gray-100 dark:hover:bg-gray-700";
  1057→  const langBtnRegex = new RegExp(
  1058→    `(onclick="setLang\\('${lang.code}'\\)" class=")${normalClass.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')}"`,
  1059→  );
  1060→  html = html.replace(langBtnRegex, `$1${highlightClass}"`);
  1061→
  1062→  // 7. Apply all string replacements (longest first for safety)
  1063→  const sorted = [...lang.strings].sort((a, b) => b[0].length - a[0].length);
  1064→  for (const [en, translated] of sorted) {
  1065→    html = html.replaceAll(en, translated);
  1066→  }
  1067→
  1068→  writeFileSync(lang.file, html, "utf-8");
  1069→  console.log(`  ✓ ${lang.file} (${html.split("\n").length} lines)`);
```
